name: Libya
change_reason: v2: long-form issue sections, private-sector coverage, podcasts, media, fact-checks
card_headline: Libya's two governments agreed a budget on paper, a UN election deal is contested, and Ukraine hit a Russian warship in Benghazi port on 22 November.
card_summary: Libya is split between the UN-recognised government of Abdulhamid Dbeibah in Tripoli and eastern authorities backed by Khalifa Haftar, whose forces hold most oilfields. Oil output reached about 1.43 million barrels a day in April, yet armed groups keep closing pipelines and striking the Zawiya refinery area. A UN-mediated election agreement signed on 30 August is disputed by the High Council of State, while a US plan would reportedly pair Dbeibah with Saddam Haftar as president. Russia, Turkey and Ukraine all operate on Libyan soil or in its waters.
card_local: Libya Herald's feed for 21 to 24 November reports that the Benghazi-based government blamed Ukraine for the explosion at Benghazi port, that the Tripoli government rejected turning Libya into an arena for foreign conflicts, and that the House of Representatives proposed a joint committee with the High Council of State. [1] Alwasat reported the Zawiya clashes in May and Libyan Express published the National Oil Corporation's April revenue figures. [2][3]
card_international: Reuters reported nine members of a Tripoli government security agency killed in a mortar blast in Zawiya on 19 October. [4] AP quoted two unnamed Libyan officials in April saying Ukrainian drone experts operate from an air base in Misrata. [5]
card_scholar: Wolfram Lacher of SWP argues that the US power-sharing push threatens a six-year stalemate and that war is the likely result whether it succeeds or fails. [6] Chatham House warns that an elite deal without fiscal conditions could deepen corruption. [7]
context_md: Libya has been unstable since Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011 and remains split between rival authorities in the west and east. [4] The October 2020 ceasefire largely ended large-scale fighting between Haftar's forces and the Tripoli-based government, but foreign-force withdrawal and security unification remain incomplete. [8] The Government of National Unity under Abdulhamid Dbeibah is the UN-recognised government, and the eastern coalition does not accept the Presidential Council headed by Mohamed al-Menfi as the final military authority. [8] Elections planned for 24 December 2021 were blocked by disputes over electoral rules and eligibility. [9] Since Haftar's 2020 bid to take Tripoli failed, his forces have controlled most of the country, including most oilfields. [6] In 2024 oil and gas made up about 65 percent of GDP, 93 percent of exports and 72 percent of government revenue, according to the World Bank as cited by the Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung. [8]

sections.title: Two governments, and a reported US plan to pair Dbeibah with Saddam Haftar
sections.body_md:
Libya has two rival administrations. Abdulhamid Dbeibah leads the UN-recognised Government of National Unity in Tripoli, and a rival government in the east is backed by Khalifa Haftar. [10] The Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung's October brief says an informal accommodation between the Dbeibah and Haftar networks sustains the equilibrium, with the balance increasingly favouring the Haftars. [8]

Massad Boulos, the US senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, is pushing a power-sharing deal. Leaked details, as relayed by Al Jazeera, would keep Dbeibah as prime minister and make Saddam Haftar president, and a summary seen by Reuters describes a 36-month transition. [10] The Financial Times reported a similar plan on 17 June, though the KAS brief says the details remain unclear. [8] Saddam Haftar met Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington in June, and the Dbeibah family did not attend. [7] As of July the Dbeibahs had not signed on. [10] Lacher reports that Misrata, the Dbeibahs' home base, has said it would mobilise against a formalised deal. [6]

The east has reshuffled too. On 6 October the House of Representatives replaced Speaker Aguila Saleh after 12 years with Al-Salhin Abdelnabi al-Obeidi, who chaired the House's Libyan-Turkish friendship committee. [11] Emadeddin Badi of Chatham House called Saleh the latest casualty of Saddam Haftar's drive to centralise decisions in the east. [11] On 20 October the House ratified the 2019 Turkey-Libya maritime memorandum, which Badi writes was condemned by the EU, Greece, Israel and Egypt. [12] The US State Department called the ratification "unhelpful and provocative." [13] On 24 November the House proposed a joint committee with the High Council of State to unify institutions. [1]

lenses.local: Libyan Express reported in May that the High Council of State rebuilt its 6+6 electoral committee amid a dispute over a member excluded from a session. [14] Libya Herald's feed carries the House's 24 November proposal for a joint committee. [1]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera, citing AFP and Reuters, reported the speaker's removal, and Al-Ahram carried the US State Department's criticism of the maritime ratification. [11][13]
lenses.scholar: Lacher argues in the New York Review of Books that the Boulos initiative endangers the six-year stalemate. [6] Chatham House's Tim Eaton says most Libyans see such a deal as a return to family rule. [10]

sections.title: The UN roadmap: an election pact signed on 30 August that the two chambers still dispute
sections.body_md:
UN envoy Hanna Tetteh presented a three-pillar roadmap to the Security Council in August 2025, covering elections, a unified government and a Structured Dialogue. [8] The dialogue ran from December 2025 to 7 June 2026, with 120 participants and more than 525 recommendations. [8] A smaller 4+4 committee, with two representatives each from the Tripoli government, the High Council of State, the House of Representatives and Haftar's Libyan National Army, first met on 29 April. [15]

On 30 August the committee agreed to restructure the board of the High National Elections Commission and to hold presidential and parliamentary elections within 24 months under one executive authority. [15][16] Dual nationals could run for president if they renounce the other nationality before taking the oath. [16] The House endorsed the agreement on 14 September, according to its spokesperson. [8] The High Council of State, led by Mohamed Takala, boycotted the signing, and on 8 September it revoked the membership of two participants who had signed without authorisation. [16][8]

Others object as well. Presidential Council head Mohamed al-Menfi criticised the procedure and foreign involvement, [16] then reappointed Imad al-Sayah as elections commission chair on 30 August although the committee had recommended Dhou Al-Hamali. [8] On 25 August 57 parties and coalitions objected to individual candidacy and the exclusion of party lists, and on 16 September Grand Mufti Sadiq al-Gharyani rejected the outcomes. [8] Turkey hosted Saleh and Takala in Ankara on 10 September, where they agreed to reactivate the 6+6 committee on electoral laws. [8] Claudia Gazzini of Crisis Group said the 4+4 risks collapsing over disagreement between the chambers. [17]

Tetteh met Dbeibah on 8 November to review the committee's work, and the government statement announced no election date. [18] The mission's mandate was due to expire on 31 October, with renewal expected. This draft did not find the Council's decision. [15] More than 2.8 million registered voters have no chance to take part in national elections, per KAS. [8]

lenses.local: Libya Herald's feed carries the US State Department's 24 November call for a unified government and credible elections, and the House's proposal for a joint committee with the High Council of State. [1]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera's 1 September report quotes one analyst saying the pact is the first signed between the active parties, and another saying outside powers are backing Saddam Haftar and Dbeibah. [16]
lenses.scholar: Carnegie's Soraya Rahem argued in December 2025 that tight timelines such as the roadmap's 12 to 18 months are largely unrealistic. [9] Crisis Group's Gazzini warns the 4+4 could collapse. [17]

sections.title: Tripoli's truce holds while the fighting and the drones move to Zawiya
sections.body_md:
In May 2025 forces loyal to Dbeibah stormed the headquarters of the Stability Support Apparatus after its leader, Abdelghani al-Kikli, known as Ghneiwa, was killed. [19] Lacher writes that the clash ended within about 24 hours and that both sides have since rebuilt their forces. [6] Asharq Al-Awsat's September 2025 map put units tied to the defence and interior ministries in the west and south of Tripoli, al-Radaa in the east, and Misrata-based militias in the buffer zones, with non-official estimates of more than 17,000 pro-Dbeibah reinforcements. [19] The UN Secretary-General's August 2026 report says the May 2025 truce held despite tensions. [20]

The 2026 fighting has been in Zawiya, about 40 km west of the capital. The UN says heavy clashes there on 8 May killed at least 13 people, with more clashes through 13 July. [20] Alwasat, citing local sources and without official confirmation, put the toll at 10 dead and 20 injured since 8 May, so the figures differ. [2] ACLED counts more than 30 armed clashes in Zawiya this year. [21] Between 8 and 11 August unclaimed drone strikes hit a naphtha tank, a desalination plant, a gasoline tank of about 4.5 million litres and two diesel tanks. [21] The National Oil Corporation declared a maximum emergency, and Dbeibah met the interior minister and armed-group chiefs. [22] UNSMIL condemned the fighting in Zawiya and Surman, where inmates escaped from a prison. [23] On 19 October nine members of the government's Anti-Threat Security Agency died in a mortar blast during a training exercise in Zawiya, according to Libya Alahrar TV as reported by Reuters. [4]

Pipelines are the next pressure point. On 21 September an armed group closed a valve on the Sharara-Zawiya pipeline, and guards blocked access to the refinery the next day. [15] In late October the NOC said another armed group had shut the Hamada pipeline to Zawiya, the second halt of flows to the refinery that month. [24] Libya Herald's feed puts the cost at about 302,778 barrels by 21 November. [1] ACLED expects escalation, including a possible offensive by forces closer to the Tripoli government that would spread beyond Zawiya. [21] The sources read for this draft report no 2026 fighting inside central Tripoli.

lenses.local: Alwasat reported the May Zawiya clashes from local sources, and Libya Herald's feed tracks the Hamada pipeline closure. [2][1]
lenses.international: Reuters reported the 19 October Zawiya blast, and Al Jazeera, citing AFP and Reuters, reported the August refinery fire. [4][22]
lenses.scholar: ACLED calls the August strikes on Zawiya unprecedented. [21] Jason Pack of Libya-Analysis LLC told The New Arab that further insecurity around the refinery is very likely if the attacks continue. [25]

sections.title: Oil output is at a multi-year high, and armed groups can still switch parts of it off
sections.body_md:
Output reached 1.43 million barrels a day in April, the highest in more than a decade, and Libya targets 2 million by 2030. [26] Dbeibah said last year's 1.37 million was a 12-year production record. [10] The National Oil Corporation aims for 1.6 million by the end of 2026. [27]

The money is large. The UN Secretary-General's report says oil and gas revenues averaged about $3.5 billion a month from April, against about $1.34 billion a month from January to March. [20] The NOC reported $2.82 billion transferred to the sovereign account at the Libyan Foreign Bank in April, with about $1.91 billion due to the Central Bank after fuel-import deductions. [3] Haftar's forces control the oilfields and terminals, while the UN recognises only the Tripoli government, so any US-brokered oil deal needs both sides. [10]

The weak point is Zawiya. Its refinery has a capacity of 120,000 barrels a day and connects to the Sharara field, which produces about 300,000. [24] The National reports that Sharara supplies about a quarter of national output, and that GE pulled its technical teams from a nearby power plant after a substation strike, leaving more than 700 MW of 1,300 MW unavailable. [27] Rystad Energy's Fiza Jan says a local incident there can become a national supply problem. [27]

Shutdowns have been a political tool since 2011. Anas El Gomati writes that Haftar's 2020 blockade cost nearly $10 billion, and that Libya exports crude but refines little, with its largest refinery offline since 2013. [28]

lenses.local: Libyan Express carries the NOC's April revenue figures, and Libya Herald's feed reports field maintenance at Hamada and a prequalification tender tied to the Erawan field. [3][1]
lenses.international: The National, citing AFP, reported the April output figure, and Al Jazeera carried Dbeibah's production-record claim. [26][10]
lenses.scholar: The Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung cites the World Bank for oil's 93 percent share of exports. [8]

sections.title: A unified budget on paper, a Central Bank under pressure, and fuel subsidies that feed armed groups
sections.body_md:
The House and the High Council of State signed a unified budget in Tripoli, and the Central Bank confirmed approval on 11 April. [29] The National puts it at 190 billion dinars, about $30 billion, the first consolidated plan since 2013. [26] Governor Naji Issa said it showed Libya is "capable of overcoming its differences." [29] Chatham House, KAS and Lacher all say it has not been meaningfully implemented. [7][8][6]

The UN Secretary-General's report describes the Central Bank's position. It began supplying more US dollars to commercial banks in April under new foreign-currency rules. The official rate stayed near 6.37 dinars to the dollar, while the parallel rate fell from 9.45 in March to about 8.5 in July. In June two Presidential Council members and the House Speaker told the bank not to authorise transactions to the General Intelligence Service. [20]

Fuel subsidies are the leak. Chatham House reports a fuel import bill above $9 billion by 2024, suppliers cut from 17 to six, and armed groups' diesel consumption up 1,527 percent against 2021. [7] The UN says fuel shortages in Tripoli and other cities were linked to illicit export of subsidised fuel, and that on 8 June the Audit Bureau and Anti-Corruption Commission reported subsidy corruption and smuggling. [20] KAS cites a UN Panel of Experts finding that Arkenu exported about 6 million barrels between May and September 2024, worth roughly $463 million, was indirectly controlled by Saddam Haftar, and bypassed Central Bank channels. [8] Al Jazeera's analysis says the Arkenu arrangement was terminated this year. [28]

The World Bank projected real GDP growth of 13.3 percent for 2025 and a fiscal surplus of 3.6 percent of GDP, and called for a Treasury Single Account. [30]

lenses.local: Libya Herald's feed reports the State Audit Bureau's 2025 annual report on 24 November and National Planning Council talks with the Central Bank on the 2027 budgets. [1]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera and Reuters reported the budget approval, and The National reported a ten-country statement welcoming it. [29][26]
lenses.scholar: Chatham House says any power-sharing deal needs enforceable transparency conditions on public finances. [7] The World Bank urges a Treasury Single Account. [30]

sections.title: Migration: departures have moved east to Cyrenaica while detention and expulsions go on
sections.body_md:
IOM estimated more than 943,748 migrants and refugees in Libya as of April 2026. Between April and July 3,393 people were intercepted at sea and 188 deaths were recorded, and 7,717 people were held in official detention centres on 19 July. [20] UNHCR had registered 110,908 people in Tripoli by the end of March, 91,494 of them Sudanese, and its Libya operation was 27 percent funded. [31]

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime reports that departures to Europe surged in 2025 to the highest level since 2017, and that in 2026 departures from western Libya collapsed as the smuggling economy shifted to Cyrenaica, with routes to Greece. [32] On 24 June the eastern-based government banned entry for nationals of Eritrea, Ethiopia, Somalia and Sudan. [20]

A joint UNSMIL and OHCHR report, covering January 2024 to November 2025, says IOM recorded 21,762 interceptions in 2024 and 27,116 in 2025, and that 3,013 people died or went missing on the central Mediterranean route in those two years. It says 4,876 people were in official centres at the end of 2025, with hundreds more in unofficial sites such as the "Osama" prison in Zawiya, and ransoms of $500 to $10,000. It reports that Frontex shared more than 2,200 geolocation messages with Libyan authorities since January 2021, that some trafficking hubs in the east appeared linked to military actors, and that at least ten international NGOs were ordered to suspend operations in April 2025. [33]

lenses.local: Libya Herald's feed lists irregular migration among topics at a 20 November forum, but no Libyan reporting on migration was read in depth for this draft. [1]
lenses.international: The UN Secretary-General's report and UNHCR's update supply the official counts. [20][31]
lenses.scholar: The Global Initiative's November analysis and the UNSMIL and OHCHR report are the main research sources. [32][33]

sections.title: Russia, Turkey, Ukraine and the US all work on Libyan ground, and Benghazi port was hit on 22 November
sections.body_md:
Africa Defense Forum, a US Africa Command publication, reported on 11 August that Russia is building or staffing infrastructure at six Libyan air bases: Maaten al-Sarra, Al-Khadim, Al-Jufra, Al-Qardabiyah, Brak al-Shati and Tamanhint. It says Russian personnel at Brak al-Shati rose from 300 to 450 after December 2024. These claims are compiled from other sources and were not independently checked. [34] In September a Russian convoy including the landing ship Aleksandr Shabalin sailed from Kaliningrad to Tobruk, and the final recipients of its cargo are uncertain. [35]

Turkey keeps a military presence in the west and sponsored the 10 September Ankara meeting. [8] Lacher calls Turkey the key external guarantor in Tripoli and says it has deepened defence ties with the Haftars, citing a Reuters report in April that Saddam's forces appear to have acquired Bayraktar TB2 drones. [6] The US held talks on 14 November between AFRICOM's commander and Dbeibah on military unification and preparations for Flintlock 2027. [36]

Ukraine has entered the picture. AP quoted two unnamed Libyan officials in April saying Ukrainian personnel, mostly drone experts, work mainly from an air base in Misrata under a covert deal with Dbeibah's government, and that the 3 March strike on the tanker Arctic Metagaz was launched from a Tripoli facility. The Tripoli government did not respond. [5] Maritime Executive notes that a Libyan Observer report denied a Ukrainian detachment at Misrata, while Ukraine acknowledged attacks on two ships. [35] Libya Herald's feed reports that the Benghazi-based government attributed a 22 November explosion at Benghazi port to a Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian vessel, that Zelenskyy claimed responsibility for the attack on the warship Mercury, and that Tripoli rejected making Libya an arena for foreign conflicts. [1]

lenses.local: Libya Herald's feed carries the Benghazi attack, UNSMIL's statement of concern and two US memoranda on aviation and rare minerals. [1]
lenses.international: AP carried the April claims about Ukrainian drone teams, and Maritime Executive recorded the Libyan denial. [5][35]
lenses.scholar: KAS and Lacher describe Turkey as a guarantor in Tripoli with growing ties to the Haftars. [8][6] The Atlantic Council's Frank Talbot, quoted by ADF, links Maaten al-Sarra to Russian operations across the Sahel. [34]

sections.title: Rights: armed groups run the prisons, disappearances continue and the ICC window closes at the end of 2027
sections.body_md:
Human Rights Watch's World Report 2026 says armed groups and security agencies run most detention facilities, with the Justice Ministry holding only nominal control. [37] It records the UN's description of enforced disappearance as a "pervasive and systematic" practice, and gives two cases: the lawmaker Ibrahim al-Drissi, abducted in May 2024 in territory held by Haftar's forces, and the activist Abdelmoneim al-Mureimi, held by a Tripoli security agency, who died in July 2025 after falling down a stairwell during interrogation. [37] Courts have confirmed 105 death sentences as of December 2024, though no executions have taken place since 2010. [37]

Armed groups fired live ammunition to disperse protesters in Tripoli in May 2025, and the Civil Society Commission can dissolve groups and freeze accounts without a court order. [37] On 10 August Fawzi al-Mansouri, head of military intelligence for Haftar's command, was killed by an explosive device outside his Benghazi home, and the perpetrators are unknown. [25]

Libya accepted ICC jurisdiction over alleged crimes from 2011 to the end of 2027. Khaled Mohamed Ali El Hishri was transferred to The Hague on 1 December 2025 and is the first suspect to face trial in the Libya investigation, while eight others, including Saif al-Islam Gaddafi, remain at large. [37] This draft did not read RSF or CPJ on press freedom, and HRW's report has no press section.

lenses.local: No Libyan outlet reporting on detention or disappearances was read for this draft.
lenses.international: HRW's World Report 2026 is the main source here, and no wire report on detention was read. [37]
lenses.scholar: Lawyers for Justice in Libya and Forensis combined survivor interviews, satellite imagery and 3D modelling in a 2025 film on the detention system. [38]

timeline.text: A NATO-led air campaign begins in Libya, and Gaddafi is overthrown that year.
A ceasefire largely halts large-scale fighting between Haftar's forces and the Tripoli-based government.
Elections set for 24 December are blocked by disputes over electoral rules and eligibility.
Killing of militia leader Ghneiwa triggers clashes in Tripoli that end in a fragile truce within about 24 hours.
UN envoy Hanna Tetteh presents a three-pillar roadmap to the Security Council.
The UN Structured Dialogue begins; it ends on 7 June 2026 with more than 525 recommendations.
The House and High Council of State sign a unified budget; the Central Bank confirms approval.
The 4+4 committee holds its first meeting.
Heavy clashes in Zawiya kill at least 13 people, per the UN.
Drone strikes set a gasoline tank alight at the Zawiya refinery complex.
The 4+4 committee agrees on elections within 24 months and a restructured elections commission.
The House of Representatives endorses the 4+4 agreement, per its spokesperson; the High Council of State rejects it.
An armed group closes a valve on the Sharara-Zawiya pipeline.
The House removes Speaker Aguila Saleh and elects Al-Salhin Abdelnabi al-Obeidi.
A mortar blast kills nine members of a government security agency in Zawiya.
The House ratifies the 2019 Turkey-Libya maritime memorandum.
Tetteh meets Dbeibah on the 4+4 committee's work; no election date is announced.
Dbeibah meets AFRICOM's commander on military unification and Flintlock 2027.
An explosion at Benghazi port is attributed to a Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian vessel; Zelenskyy claims the attack on the warship Mercury on 23 November.
The House proposes a joint committee with the High Council of State to unify institutions; the US State Department renews its call for a unified government and credible elections.

reporters.name: Wolfram Lacher
reporters.role: Senior Associate, German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP)
reporters.bio: Wrote the 5 August 2026 New York Review of Books essay on the US-brokered mediation effort, and the 2020 book Libya's Fragmentation: Structure and Process in Violent Conflict.
reporters.why: His essay argues the Boulos initiative threatens a six-year stalemate and that war is the likely outcome whether it succeeds or fails.
reporters.label: The New York Review of Books

reporters.name: Claudia Gazzini
reporters.role: Senior Libya analyst, International Crisis Group
reporters.bio: Described by Agenzia Nova as Crisis Group's senior Libya analyst and by the Hold Your Fire! podcast page as its Libya expert.
reporters.why: Warned that the 4+4 agreement risks collapsing over disagreement between the two chambers.
reporters.label: Agenzia Nova

reporters.name: Emadeddin Badi
reporters.role: Analyst, identified by Al Jazeera as of Chatham House
reporters.bio: Wrote the 26 October 2026 Al Jazeera opinion piece on Saddam Haftar and was quoted in Al Jazeera's report on the speaker's removal.
reporters.why: Traces how the removal of Speaker Saleh and the maritime ratification fit Saddam Haftar's push to centralise power in the east.
reporters.label: Al Jazeera

reporters.name: Tim Eaton
reporters.bio: Quoted by Al Jazeera on 8 July 2026 on the US mediation plan.
reporters.why: Says the deal depends on the Haftar and Dbeibah families agreeing, and that most Libyans see it as a return to family rule.
reporters.label: Al Jazeera

reporters.name: Frederic Wehrey
reporters.role: Senior fellow, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace
reporters.bio: Author of The Burning Shores: Inside the Battle for the New Libya (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2018), listed by Publishers Weekly; quoted by The New Arab in August 2026.
reporters.why: Argues that local armed actors can undermine deals struck among a narrow elite, as Zawiya showed.
reporters.label: The New Arab

reporters.name: Anas El Gomati
reporters.role: Analyst, Sadeq Institute (as named by The New Arab)
reporters.bio: Wrote the 21 August 2026 Al Jazeera analysis of Libya's rivals bargaining over economic issues.
reporters.why: Documents how factions have used oil shutdowns as a bargaining tool and how fuel subsidies feed smuggling.
reporters.label: Al Jazeera

reporters.name: Matt Herbert, Rupert Horsley and Henry Harbottle
reporters.role: Researchers, Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime
reporters.bio: Listed as the authors of the Libya report in the Global Initiative's 2026 smuggling and trafficking series, posted 18 November 2026.
reporters.why: Their work tracks the shift of the smuggling economy from western Libya to Cyrenaica.
reporters.label: Global Initiative

reporters.name: Fareed Rahman
reporters.bio: Byline on the 13 August 2026 report on drone strikes at the Zawiya refinery.
reporters.why: Quotes energy analysts at Rystad and Kpler on how a local incident can become a national supply problem.
reporters.label: The National

books.why: Publishers Weekly reviewed it in May 2012 as a study of Qaddafi's rule and the 2011 uprising. The year is inferred from that review date.

factchecks.claim: Libya now has a unified national budget that has brought the east and west together.
factchecks.by: Headlines and a joint statement of ten governments welcoming the April 2026 budget
factchecks.evidence: The House and High Council of State signed a 190 billion dinar budget in April, the first since 2013. Chatham House says it has not been meaningfully implemented, KAS says it has not produced effective fiscal unification, and Lacher says neither the November 2025 nor the April 2026 deal shows signs of implementation.

scores.coverage_basis: Reuters, AP and AFP file on Libya mainly when something breaks, such as the Zawiya refinery fire or the Ukrainian drone claims [4][5][22]. Think-tank output is steady from Chatham House, ACLED, KAS and the Global Initiative [7][21][8][32], and Libya Herald publishes daily in English [1].

severity.basis: Zawiya saw at least 13 killed on 8 May and unclaimed drone strikes on the refinery in August, while the May 2025 Tripoli truce has held [20][21].
More than 943,748 migrants and refugees are in Libya, 7,717 are in official detention, and UNHCR's operation was 27 percent funded [20][31].
Armed groups run most detention facilities, the UN calls enforced disappearance pervasive and systematic, and no national election has been held since the 2021 vote was blocked [37][9].
Oil revenue has risen to about $3.5 billion a month, but 93 percent of exports are oil, the parallel dinar trades well above the official rate, and fuel subsidies are widely diverted [20][8].
The 4+4 pact and unified budget are steps forward on paper, but the House removed its speaker, pipelines are being shut and Lacher expects war if the US plan fails [11][15][6].

parts.basis: The US is mediating with an oil-investment offer, Russia is reported at six air bases, Turkey keeps forces in the west and Ukraine claimed an attack at Benghazi port [10][34][8][1].
Output near 1.43 million barrels a day and Africa's largest proven reserves, with tankers two days from Italy, give Libya weight in European energy supply [26][10].
ADF reports Al-Khadim used to deliver weapons to Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, and GI-TOC reports a surge in departures to Europe and a shift of routes to Greece [34][32].
About 943,748 migrants and refugees are in Libya, and 3,013 people died or went missing on the central Mediterranean route in 2024 and 2025 [20][33].
Libya accepted ICC jurisdiction to the end of 2027, and the maritime memorandum and the strikes on Russian vessels in Libyan ports test sea-law claims and neutrality [37][12][1].

summary: Libya matters beyond its borders through oil, the Mediterranean migration route and its use as a base by Russia, Turkey and now Ukraine [26][32][35].
The score is held down because a UN-recognised government still functions in Tripoli, large-scale war has not resumed since 2020, and the economy is small outside oil [8][20].
gi.up: Collapse of the Tripoli truce, a Haftar-Dbeibah deal that Misrata rejects by force, or a prolonged shutdown of Zawiya and Sharara.
gi.down: A funded and implemented unified budget, a signed unified government and a dated election.

gaps: Local sourcing is partial: Libya Herald was read only through feed summaries, and Alwasat and Libyan Express were each read for one or two articles. Libya Observer, Libya Review, Libya Update, Libya Desk and the state news agency LANA could not be opened (not on the fetch allowlist or not surfaced by search), so none is cited.

No opened outlet could be shown to be aligned with Tripoli or the east. The alignment of Alwasat, Libyan Express and Libya Herald was not checked, and none is flagged as state_affiliated. Al Jazeera, Al-Ahram, ADF and QNA are flagged for their own state ties, not for a Libyan side.

The 22 to 24 November events (Benghazi port attack, Zelenskyy's claim, Tripoli's and Benghazi's statements, the House initiative, the US State Department call) rest on Libya Herald feed summaries; no wire copy or article page was opened.
The outcome of the Security Council's October 2026 renewal of the UNSMIL mandate was not found.
No 2026 fighting inside central Tripoli appears in the sources read; this may reflect search coverage, not absence.
Zawiya death tolls differ between the UN (at least 13 on 8 May) and Alwasat (10 dead since 8 May, local sources); the Alwasat figure is unconfirmed.
The parallel dinar rate differs across The National (under 7), the UN (about 8.5 in July) and Al Jazeera (above 9 in August); not resolved.
The UN Panel of Experts, the Crisis Group Libya reports and the IMF were cited only through secondary pages (KAS, Agenzia Nova, The National); the primary documents were not opened.
Claims about Russian air bases come from ADF, a US military publication that compiles other sources, and are not independently verified.
RSF and CPJ on press freedom were not read; HRW's report has no press section. No Libyan reporter or editor could be verified, so the reporters list is analysts and foreign reporters only.
The Chatham House July piece is an unsigned expert comment. The podcast and documentary links point to listing pages and availability varies by country.

local_md:
Libyan Express reported in May that the High Council of State rebuilt its 6+6 electoral committee amid a dispute over a member excluded from a session. [14] Libya Herald's feed carries the House's 24 November proposal for a joint committee. [1]

Libya Herald's feed carries the US State Department's 24 November call for a unified government and credible elections, and the House's proposal for a joint committee with the High Council of State. [1]

Alwasat reported the May Zawiya clashes from local sources, and Libya Herald's feed tracks the Hamada pipeline closure. [2][1]

Libyan Express carries the NOC's April revenue figures, and Libya Herald's feed reports field maintenance at Hamada and a prequalification tender tied to the Erawan field. [3][1]

Libya Herald's feed reports the State Audit Bureau's 2025 annual report on 24 November and National Planning Council talks with the Central Bank on the 2027 budgets. [1]

Libya Herald's feed lists irregular migration among topics at a 20 November forum, but no Libyan reporting on migration was read in depth for this draft. [1]

Libya Herald's feed carries the Benghazi attack, UNSMIL's statement of concern and two US memoranda on aviation and rare minerals. [1]

No Libyan outlet reporting on detention or disappearances was read for this draft.
international_md:
Al Jazeera, citing AFP and Reuters, reported the speaker's removal, and Al-Ahram carried the US State Department's criticism of the maritime ratification. [11][13]

Al Jazeera's 1 September report quotes one analyst saying the pact is the first signed between the active parties, and another saying outside powers are backing Saddam Haftar and Dbeibah. [16]

Reuters reported the 19 October Zawiya blast, and Al Jazeera, citing AFP and Reuters, reported the August refinery fire. [4][22]

The National, citing AFP, reported the April output figure, and Al Jazeera carried Dbeibah's production-record claim. [26][10]

Al Jazeera and Reuters reported the budget approval, and The National reported a ten-country statement welcoming it. [29][26]

The UN Secretary-General's report and UNHCR's update supply the official counts. [20][31]

AP carried the April claims about Ukrainian drone teams, and Maritime Executive recorded the Libyan denial. [5][35]

HRW's World Report 2026 is the main source here, and no wire report on detention was read. [37]
scholar_md:
Lacher argues in the New York Review of Books that the Boulos initiative endangers the six-year stalemate. [6] Chatham House's Tim Eaton says most Libyans see such a deal as a return to family rule. [10]

Carnegie's Soraya Rahem argued in December 2025 that tight timelines such as the roadmap's 12 to 18 months are largely unrealistic. [9] Crisis Group's Gazzini warns the 4+4 could collapse. [17]

ACLED calls the August strikes on Zawiya unprecedented. [21] Jason Pack of Libya-Analysis LLC told The New Arab that further insecurity around the refinery is very likely if the attacks continue. [25]

The Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung cites the World Bank for oil's 93 percent share of exports. [8]

Chatham House says any power-sharing deal needs enforceable transparency conditions on public finances. [7] The World Bank urges a Treasury Single Account. [30]

The Global Initiative's November analysis and the UNSMIL and OHCHR report are the main research sources. [32][33]

KAS and Lacher describe Turkey as a guarantor in Tripoli with growing ties to the Haftars. [8][6] The Atlantic Council's Frank Talbot, quoted by ADF, links Maaten al-Sarra to Russian operations across the Sahel. [34]

Lawyers for Justice in Libya and Forensis combined survivor interviews, satellite imagery and 3D modelling in a 2025 film on the detention system. [38]
